name: Hanging for neck decompression

lead: Hanging for neck decompression means using a bar, band or door-mounted unit to gently pull on the neck and relieve tightness.
Lifters describe it as feeling good and helping them keep training comfortably, which supports posture and physique.

paras: Traction is meant to separate vertebrae slightly and stretch soft tissue around the neck; self-applied versions use body weight or a band.
Clinical traction is supervised; home use is not standardised. People with neck pain or nerve symptoms are typically advised to be assessed first.

chain: Gentle traction or hanging relieves neck and upper-back tightness
Greater comfort and mobility in training and daily posture
angle.text: People use neck decompression and hanging to ease tension that builds up from lifting or desk posture. The looks link is indirect: a looser neck and shoulder region can support better head carriage and continued training.

lead: Hanging for neck decompression refers to the practice of using body weight, a harness, a door-mounted traction unit or an elastic band to apply gentle traction to the neck, with the aim of relieving stiffness and tension. In training communities it is discussed as a way to ease a tight neck and shoulders, which supports continued lifting and posture work, and so a stronger, more upright-looking frame.[1][2][3]

Forum users describe a range of methods. One T Nation user described a video technique of placing a band behind the neck and leaning back across each vertebra, another bought an over-the-door neck traction unit as an alternative to physiotherapy visits, and others mention hanging from a bar or captain's chair as feeling good for the back.[1][2][3] Neck harness work for strength is a separate practice.

Mechanical spinal traction is a studied physical-therapy approach. Wikipedia describes it as intended to separate vertebral bodies, move facet joints, widen the spaces nerves exit through and stretch soft tissue, and reviews describe it as useful in combination with other physical therapy for pain in the cervical or lumbar spine, with guidelines resting on low-quality evidence.[4][5] Studies of self-applied hanging or home neck units were not found.
infobox: Bar, harness, band, over-the-door traction unit

paras: Practitioners described on lifting forums use several approaches: hanging passively from a bar or dip station or a captain's chair, using a band around the back of the neck while leaning back, or an over-the-door traction device that pulls on the neck.[1][2][3] Users say it feels like it decompresses the area.[3]

The practices differ in how the pull is delivered. Bar hanging uses body weight acting on the spine and shoulders, whereas door-mounted units and bands apply a pull to the head and neck specifically. None of these is described in the clinical literature as a standard protocol.

Wikipedia describes traction as the application of pulling force to the body, and notes that many traction procedures have largely been replaced by more modern techniques; it shows a traction device from a Byzantine edition of Galen's work, dating to the 2nd century AD, as an early example.[4] Mechanical traction is delivered through an apparatus in intermittent or continuous modes, with indications including cervical radiculopathy, lumbar spinal stenosis and other cervical and lumbar disorders.[4]

Non-surgical spinal decompression is a related term. Wikipedia defines spinal decompression as relief of pressure on the spinal cord or compressed nerve roots, lists traction as a non-surgical option, and cites a 2007 paper that questioned whether the scientific literature supports advertising claims for non-surgical decompression.[5]

A 2018 systematic review (Romeo and colleagues) looked at adding traction to physical therapy in cervical radiculopathy, and a 2020 review (Colombo and colleagues) reported mechanical traction outperforming manual traction and continuous outperforming intermittent, with the pain effect described as statistically significant but not clinically relevant. Guidelines by Kjaer and colleagues in 2017 described the evidence for cervical traction as low quality and called for more research.[4] A 2021 meta-analysis found physiotherapy effective for lumbar disc prolapse, and a 2022 meta-analysis found mechanical traction better than conventional physiotherapy in the short term, over weeks, though not in all studies beyond six months.[5] These studies concern clinician-delivered or clinic-based traction rather than home hanging.

Clinical neck traction is applied with neurovascular checks and prescribed settings.[4] Self-applied hanging is not standardised, and people with neck or nerve symptoms are generally directed by clinicians to seek assessment before using traction.

On T Nation the topic appears incidentally. A 2010 training-log thread includes a suggestion that people carry stress in the neck, shoulders and back, with the poster saying hanging on a captain's chair sometimes feels very good.[2] A 2012 log mentions buying a door-mounted neck decompression unit so as not to need physiotherapy appointments for neck traction.[3] A 2017 log shares a band-based neck decompression video that the poster found felt good.[1] Neck-strength work with harnesses is a separate topic in the same communities.
No studies found on self-directed hanging specifically. Studies of clinical mechanical traction, a related practice, are described above.[4][5]
